title: Departure from the 21164: out-of-order execution combined with high clock frequency
decision: The 21264 was designed as an out-of-order, speculative processor with a large instruction window, deliberately departing from its predecessor the 21164, which issued in-order.
alternatives_or_rejected: The implicit alternative rejected was the 21164's in-order, statically scheduled, frequency-first approach; my recollection is the paper argues for out-of-order rather than formally tabulating rejected options.
rationale: The paper's stated position is that an in-order machine could not extract enough instruction-level parallelism from real code to reach the performance targets, and that out-of-order execution could be reconciled with, rather than traded against, very high clock frequency.
outcome: The paper presents the aggressive out-of-order design as the central reason for the 21264's large performance gains over the 21164 on both integer and floating-point code.

title: Combined local + global branch predictor with a chooser
decision: The 21264 uses a hybrid branch predictor combining a local history component (local history table indexed into a local predictor), a global-history component, and a chooser table that selects between them; fetch is also redirected only on taken branches.
alternatives_or_rejected: Simpler single-component predictors (e.g., bimodal-only as in earlier designs) are the implicit alternative; I do not recall the paper detailing an explicit list of rejected predictor designs.
rationale: Combining local and global history captures both branch-specific and correlated behavior, giving higher accuracy, which matters because the cost of mispredictions is high in the deep out-of-order pipeline. Specific table sizes (on the order of 1024-entry local histories, 4096-entry global and chooser tables) are recalled with moderate certainty.
outcome: The paper reports low misprediction rates on its benchmark set, supporting the aggressive fetch/window design.

title: Memory dependence speculation: loads execute before older stores' addresses are known
where_in_paper: Memory system / load-store execution discussion (memory reorder buffer)
decision: Loads are allowed to execute speculatively ahead of older stores whose addresses are not yet resolved; a memory reorder buffer (32 entries, as I recall) tracks outstanding memory operations, and a dependence misprediction triggers a replay of the affected instructions.
alternatives_or_rejected: The conservative alternative is to stall loads until all older store addresses are known; I do not recall the paper presenting a formal rejection of this, but the speculation-with-replay scheme is presented as deliberate.
rationale: Conservatively ordering every load against every unresolved store would forfeit much of the parallelism the large out-of-order window is meant to expose; speculation plus replay only pays the penalty on the (rare) mispredictions.
outcome: The paper reports that this enables high memory-level parallelism while preserving correct memory ordering, with replays occurring rarely enough not to undermine performance.

title: No on-chip secondary cache: large on-chip L1s plus a large off-chip L2
decision: Unlike the 21164 (which had an on-chip secondary cache), the 21264 uses relatively large on-chip first-level caches (64 KB each, as I recall) and a multi-megabyte secondary cache located off-chip.
alternatives_or_rejected: The 21164-style on-chip L2 was the alternative; the trade-off is spending die area on the second-level cache versus on the L1 capacity and the out-of-order machinery. I recall the paper discussing this trade-off but am less certain how explicitly it frames the on-chip-L2 option as considered and rejected.
rationale: On the target process, area was judged better spent on the large L1s and the big instruction window than on an on-chip L2, with the large external L2 preserving cache capacity.
outcome: The paper reports the resulting hierarchy sustains the bandwidth/latency behavior the out-of-order core needs, at the cost of a multi-cycle off-chip L2 access.

title: Register renaming into physical register files (80 integer / 72 FP), with a replicated integer register file across clusters
where_in_paper: Register renaming / integer issue and execution-cluster discussion
decision: Speculative results are held in enlarged physical register files (80 integer and 72 floating-point physical registers, numbers I recall from the paper) rather than in a reorder buffer; the integer physical register file is replicated across the two integer execution clusters, and integer issue is handled by separate per-cluster queues with oldest-ready-first arbitration.
alternatives_or_rejected: ROB-based buffering of speculative results and a single centralized, highly multi-ported integer register file/queue are the implicit alternatives; the port-count and cycle-time argument for replication and split queues is my recollection, and I am not certain the paper explicitly names the monolithic design as a rejected option.
rationale: Providing enough register read ports for multiple integer instructions per cycle from one monolithic file would be slow and complex; replicating the file per cluster keeps each cluster's read local and the cycle time short. A large pool of physical registers supports the big out-of-order window.
outcome: The paper reports the clustered organization sustains wide integer issue and the intended clock frequency, with the register map checkpoint/rename mechanism handling misprediction recovery.
